section_summary: This section contains U.S. State Department correspondence and internal memoranda from February and March 1938 focusing on internal political developments, military discipline, and the centralization of state authority in Japan. It features comprehensive reporting on the National General Mobilization Bill, including ambassadorial analysis and press transcripts of contentious Diet committee deliberations in which Premier Fumimaro Konoe defended the government's sweeping enabling powers against accusations of totalitarianism and unconstitutionality. The documents also examine an imperial amnesty restoring civil rights to participants in political revolts and canceling punishments for army infractions in China, as well as an interview given by General Sadao Araki to The Japan Advertiser that prompted harassment by reactionary ruffians intent on preserving his standing to lead a future fascist single-party movement.

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on political controversy surrounding the National Mobilization Act and demands for Home Minister Suetsugu's resignation.
subfiles.summary: Closing section of Telegram No. 149: measures restricting liberties arouse suspicion of Home Minister Suetsugu's totalitarian designs; parties demand his resignation, but Konoe unlikely to dismiss him and no crisis expected during the China war.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 149 from Tokyo regarding Political Tension and the National Mobilization Act

subfiles.about: A Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum calling attention to a Shanghai despatch regarding the cancellation of Japanese military disciplinary punishments.
subfiles.summary: Memo notes marked passages in a Shanghai despatch on an Army order canceling earlier disciplinary punishments, apparently including soldiers punished in China; the clipping adds nothing.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Shanghai Despatch Regarding Cancellation of Army Punishments

subfiles.about: Consul General Gauss transmits a press report concerning a Japanese army order canceling punishment of soldiers, noting its relevance to offenses against Americans in China.
subfiles.summary: Gauss forwards a clipping on the Empire Day amnesty restoring rights to 300,000, including February 26 and May 15 rebels, and an Army order canceling punishments, relevant to offenses against Americans.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1212: Announcement in Tokyo of Cancellation of Army Order of Punishment

subfiles.about: A Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum commenting on Tokyo Despatch No. 2800 regarding the Economic Mobilization Bill.
subfiles.summary: Jones says Despatch No. 2800 on the Economic Mobilization Bill adds little, and the translated text was amended twice before enactment.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 2800 Regarding the Economic Mobilization Bill

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits and analyzes the Japanese Government's National General Mobilization Bill and enclosed press accounts of Diet committee debates.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits an English translation and comprehensive analysis of the National General Mobilization Bill presented to the Diet, which confers sweeping authority to mobilize human and economic resources through imperial ordinances during wartime or similar incidents. Grew examines constitutional issues under Articles 5, 31, and 70 of the Meiji Constitution, noting widespread domestic unease that the measure establishes a totalitarian regime and bypasses parliamentary oversight. He recounts Premier Fumimaro Konoe's appearance before a Lower House committee on March 2, where Konoe defended the constitutionality of the legislation, denied fascist intentions, and sought to quell opposition. Enclosures provide the full 50-article draft translation from The Japan Advertiser of February 20, 1938, as well as a detailed stenographic report of committee interpellations from March 3, 1938.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2800: Economic Mobilization Bill

subfiles.about: An informal State Department routing slip recommending the reading of a full newspaper article concerning General Araki rather than its digest.
subfiles.summary: Routing slip to Mr. Green advising reading the original Araki article rather than the digest (Despatch No. 2798).
subfiles.title: State Department Routing Slip Regarding Article on General Araki

subfiles.about: A Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum analyzing Tokyo Despatch No. 2798 regarding General Sadao Araki's interview with The Japan Advertiser and its political repercussions.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine on Despatch No. 2798: Araki's interview with The Japan Advertiser says Japan joined the Anti-Comintern Pact only for anti-communist expediency; ruffians then coerced the journalists into publishing clarifications.
subfiles.title: State Department Memorandum on Despatch No. 2798 Regarding Interview with General Araki

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports on General Sadao Araki's interview with The Japan Advertiser, the intimidation of journalists by political ruffians, and encloses the published text.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew details the background and aftermath of an interview granted by General Sadao Araki to American correspondents Frank Hedges and Oland D. Russell, published under the headline 'Japan's Link to Fascism Expediency, Says Araki.' After publication, Russell and his interpreter were summoned to Araki's residence and subjected to physical intimidation by organized reactionary ruffians who insisted on drafting a published clarification affirming spiritual ties with Germany and Italy. Grew explains that extreme right-wing groups sought to keep Araki's record untainted by anti-fascist remarks so he could serve as figurehead for a single authoritarian party displacing parliamentary factions. The enclosed clipping from The Japan Advertiser of February 4, 1938, contains Araki's extensive remarks on the Anti-Comintern Pact, the Treaty of Versailles, Emperor Meiji's Rescript, the spiritual superiority of the Way of Japan over Western legalism, and reports of atrocities in China.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2798: Interview with General Sadao Araki Concerning Japan's Link to Fascism
